title: “YOUR TWO BREASTS ARE LIKE TWO FAWNS”: Why Would God Put THAT in the Bible?
paragraphs: “YOUR TWO BREASTS ARE LIKE TWO FAWNS”: Why Would God Put THAT in the Bible?
The verse some Christians rush past may expose something far deeper than sexuality—and reveal what sin distorted, what shame buried, and what Jesus came to redeem.
There are verses we print on coffee mugs, hang above fireplaces, whisper beside hospital beds, and post beneath sunsets.
And then there are verses we hope nobody asks us about.
Song of Songs 4:5 is one of them.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.”
Not hidden in some obscure manuscript.
Not inserted by a modern translator trying to be provocative.
And the original Hebrew does not rescue embarrassed readers by making the language less direct.
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ‘ofarim, te’omei tseviyyah, haro‘im bashoshanim.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns…”
The Hebrew noun שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) really does refer to “your breasts.”
So we cannot explain the verse away.
And perhaps the reason this verse makes some Christians uncomfortable is not because Scripture has become inappropriate.
Perhaps it is because sin has taught us to see something God created through eyes distorted by shame, exploitation, pornography, lust, insecurity, comparison, abuse, and fear.
The question is no longer merely, “Why would God allow breasts to be mentioned in Scripture?”
What happened to us that we can read about murder, betrayal, warfare, crucifixion, greed, demons, judgment, adultery, and human depravity without blinking…
but when Scripture describes the beauty of the human body within the poetry of covenant love, suddenly we become uncomfortable?
Because this is not really an article about breasts.
It is about what happened to beauty after Eden.
It is about what happened to intimacy after sin.
It is about the difference between desire and exploitation.
It is about the difference between seeing someone and consuming someone.
And ultimately, it is about a Savior who does not merely forgive sinners.
Jesus begins restoring what sin shattered.
Before shame entered the human story, Genesis gives us an astonishing sentence:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Those two realities once existed together.
There was a time in human history when the body was not merchandise.
No person staring into a mirror wondering whether their body was worthy of being loved.
No man secretly training his eyes to consume women.
No woman believing her value depended upon whether men desired her.
No wounded spouse wondering why she was no longer enough.
No child growing up carrying shame because someone violated what should have been protected.
Genesis 3 says their eyes were opened, they realized they were naked, and they covered themselves.
The body had not suddenly become evil.
Christianity does not teach that the physical body is inherently dirty.
And God looked upon His creation and declared it “very good.”
The tragedy is not that humanity possesses bodies.
The tragedy is what fallen humanity has learned to do with them.
We despise ourselves when we believe we do not possess enough of it.
We take something designed to participate in covenant intimacy and turn it into entertainment.
Then, after generations of sexual brokenness, we sometimes open Song of Songs and act surprised that God is willing to speak about embodied love.
But Scripture refuses to surrender human sexuality to pornography.
It refuses to let lust have the final definition of desire.
It refuses to let exploitation have the final word about the body.
And that is part of why Song of Songs matters.
It contains longing, admiration, beauty, desire, separation, pursuit, delight, and commitment expressed through the imagery of the ancient world.
When the beloved is compared to fawns, lilies, doves, gardens, towers, spices, fruit, and fountains, we are entering poetry—not an anatomy textbook.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle…”
Symmetry—the text specifically calls them twins.
Something contemplated poetically rather than described crudely.
The imagery belongs to a world of gardens, animals, fragrance, vineyards, lilies, springtime, and flourishing life.
Because biblical poetry communicates through pictures.
When Song of Songs 4:4 compares the woman’s neck to “the tower of David,” nobody imagines that her neck was literally made from masonry.
When her teeth are compared to a flock of sheep, nobody imagines wool growing from her mouth.
When her lips are compared with scarlet thread, nobody imagines sewing material attached to her face.
So when the poem describes her breasts as twin fawns grazing among lilies, the writer is not offering crude anatomical commentary.
He is communicating beauty through the language of tenderness, harmony, delicacy, and delight.
The woman is not merely a body in Song of Songs.
There is mutuality throughout the poetry.
That is profoundly different from pornography.
Pornography asks, “How can this body satisfy me?”
Covenant love asks, “How can I cherish this person?”
Pornography separates the body from personhood.
Biblical love refuses to do that.
Love learns to behold without dehumanizing.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that distinction hurts.
Maybe pornography has been your secret for years.
Your children certainly do not know.
You know how to delete the history.
You know how to close the browser.
You know how to promise God, “Never again.”
And somewhere along the way you began wondering whether God was disgusted with you.
Jesus does not call lust harmless.
Christ's standard goes deeper than outward adultery. In Matthew 5:28, He exposes lust in the heart itself.
So grace does not mean pretending your bondage is innocent.
Grace means your bondage does not have to become your identity.
Repentance does not say, “It doesn't matter.”
Repentance says, “It matters so much that I am bringing it into the light.”
Maybe pornography is not your story.
Maybe you have spent years hating your body.
You compare yourself with edited photographs.
You have stood in front of a mirror and silently insulted someone made in the image of God.
Perhaps somebody once mocked your body.
Perhaps someone you loved compared you with another person.
Perhaps someone touched you in a way they never had the right to.
And now even beautiful biblical language about the body makes something inside you tense.
Song of Songs does not teach that physical beauty determines human worth.
It does show us something our wounded culture desperately needs to recover:
embodied human love does not have to be dirty.
Beauty does not have to become an idol.
Desire does not have to become exploitation.
Sexuality does not have to become pornography.
The body does not have to become merchandise.
And marriage does not have to become emotionally lifeless simply because Christians are frightened of acknowledging attraction.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure.
Purity, biblically understood, is not the annihilation of marital desire.
God calls His people toward a holiness capable of governing desire rather than pretending desire does not exist.
And here is where we must be careful.

Song of Songs is first and directly a collection of human love poetry. Christians through the centuries have also found echoes in its language that remind them of God's covenant love and, by theological extension, Christ's love for His people.
But we do not need to erase the human love poem to make the book spiritual.
God is not embarrassed by what He inspired.
Yet every beautiful thing in Scripture eventually confronts us with the tragedy of the Fall.
Because we know love is not always like this.
Abuse turns places that should have been safe into places of terror.
Some people reading these words have discovered messages on a spouse's phone that changed their lives forever.
Some have watched the person who promised “until death do us part” walk away.
Others carry wounds somebody committed against them.
And suddenly Song of Songs does not feel romantic anymore.
It feels like evidence from another world.
A world where love has not yet broken.
And that is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus entered our broken world.
The God who created human bodies did not rescue humanity by despising embodiment.
The Son took on human flesh.
His hands and feet were pierced.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
Christian redemption is not God saying matter never mattered.
The resurrection announces that God's answer to human brokenness is bigger than escaping creation.
He is making all things new.
That includes the sinner who thinks sexual sin has permanently disqualified him.
The woman who believes shame has permanently named her.
The husband who has been hiding.
The wife who has been wounded.
The person who has confused attention with love.
The believer whose private browser history contradicts his public worship.
But it can also become the beginning of freedom.
Because the Christ who knows the entire truth about you is the Christ who went to the cross for sinners.
You do not have to clean yourself enough to become eligible for mercy.
Not grace that baptizes bondage and calls it freedom.
Grace that forgives and then teaches us how to walk differently.
Grace that says your worst chapter does not get naming rights over the rest of your story.
The woman caught in adultery knew public shame.
The Samaritan woman knew relational brokenness.
Paul knew what it meant to have a past he could never undo.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose histories should have destroyed them.
Not good people becoming slightly better.
And perhaps that is why this strange, beautiful, uncomfortable verse belongs in your Bible.
Because God refuses to surrender any territory of human existence to the enemy.
Christ lays claim to all of you.
The parts you show at church.
And the parts you hide when everyone goes home.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“What has sin taught me to see that Jesus wants to teach me to see differently?”
That question reaches far beyond Song of Songs.
How do you see your spouse?
How do you see your own body?
How do you see people whose bodies attract you?
Or as human beings carrying the image of their Creator?
And what are you feeding your eyes when nobody is watching?
Because there are moments when the most spiritual thing you can do is stop pretending.
Maybe tonight needs to become the night the secret ends.
Because Christ is worthy of the room you have kept locked.
Tell Him the truth He already knows.
“Jesus, I have used people in my imagination.”
“Jesus, I have hated the body You gave me.”
“Jesus, I have carried shame for something somebody did to me.”
“Jesus, I have confused lust with love.”
And then remember why there is a cross.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
But scandal does not get the final word.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write your private details publicly. But if you want to mark this moment, comment, “No more hiding.”
If you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your heart has been wounded and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you have already watched Jesus begin restoring something you thought could never be restored, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting.
That comment might become somebody else's courage to come into the light.
Not because every Christian needs another post on a timeline.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
We want to go where the text goes.
Scripture gives a real basis for believers voluntarily supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work in 1 Corinthians 9:14.
But Scripture also protects the heart of giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says giving must not be reluctant or compelled.
It does not purchase God's favor.
Your support helps keep the message moving.
More opportunities for one wounded person scrolling alone at midnight to encounter Scripture when they were about to surrender to despair.
Send it to the person God brought to your mind while you were reading.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is hiding.
Somebody thinks their secret has made them unreachable.
Somebody thinks their marriage is too broken.
Somebody has confused being desired with being loved.
Somebody is wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
And the answer of the cross is not that sin does not matter.
The answer is that Jesus went far enough to save sinners from it.
The body sin taught you to objectify was created by God.
The sexuality culture taught you to worship belongs under the lordship of Christ.
The shame that told you to hide can be dragged into the light.
The sin that whispers, “This is who you are,” does not have authority to rewrite what Jesus has redeemed.
Song of Songs 4:5 is not an embarrassing mistake God forgot to edit out of Scripture.
It belongs inside a Bible that tells the truth about being human.
A Bible containing gardens and graves.
And standing at the center of that entire story is not human sexuality.
Maybe you opened this because a verse about “two breasts” caught your attention.
Maybe God used the uncomfortable verse to bring you somewhere far more uncomfortable:
The Savior already knows what is there.
Bring Him the body you hate.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Because the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
It is that He can take a life marked by scandal and write grace across pages you thought were ruined forever.
Your shame may remember the old chapter—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still writing the next one.
